 We’re taking a phased approach to expanding Autopilot across Microsoft, giving our employees access to an always-on personal agent with its own identity that keeps work moving even when they’re offline. 
 Launching the personal agent era: How we’re rolling out Autopilot at Microsoft
 November 19, 2026 
 |
 Alex Fleck 
 First came Microsoft Copilot. Then came agents. Now, we’re giving employees at Microsoft personal agents of their own.
 Autopilot, released this fall, is one of the first enterprise-ready personal agents. It isn’t a tool you open and close. It’s an always-on personal agent with its own identity and lifecycle, and it keeps working when its sponsor is offline. Employees reach Autopilot the way they’d reach a colleague, through Microsoft Teams and Outlook, as well as in the Copilot app.
 We began our Autopilot journey at Microsoft a few months ago with a voluntary deployment to a small group of employees. From there, we’re taking a phased approach to expanding availability across the company, giving leaders flexibility to determine when deployment makes sense for their organization based on their plans, schedules, and budgets.
 Personal agents represent a new challenge for us in Microsoft Digital, the company’s IT organization. Every Autopilot is a real identity in our tenant, with its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID (an agent user in Entra), its own Outlook mailbox, and its own OneDrive for storage. Each one lists the employee who sponsors it as its manager, so it shows up as one of that person’s direct reports.
 That means we have to manage them with the same rigor we apply to employee identities, not as short-lived tools.
 “We’ve managed identities for people and devices for decades. Agents are the next identity, and they’re already doing real work across Microsoft. As Customer Zero, we’re working through this new frontier ourselves so we can share what we learn with customers.”
 Tal Saraf, corporate vice president and chief technology and AI officer, Microsoft 
 Scale is where it gets hard.
 At pilot scale, temporary, internal solutions can keep things running. At company scale, each Autopilot is another identity to provision, secure, audit, review, and eventually retire, and soon there could be one for every employee. That’s why we’re testing how identity volume affects Microsoft Exchange, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams, and why we want these controls to live in the product rather than in custom IT workarounds.
 There’s no established playbook for running personal agents across an entire workforce, so we’re writing ours now and sharing it as we go.
 “We’ve managed identities for people and devices for decades. Agents are the next identity, and they’re already doing real work across Microsoft,” says Tal Saraf, corporate vice president and chief technology and AI officer at Microsoft. “As Customer Zero, we’re working through this new frontier ourselves so we can share what we learn with customers.”
 Get ready for Autopilot
 Join our Frontier program to get early access to new Copilot capabilities, including Autopilot, as they become available. 
 A new kind of participant in the enterprise
 As we introduce Autopilot to our employees, it’s important to understand where it fits into enterprise AI workflows. The distinction is easiest to understand through the work that each experience—Copilot Chat, Cowork, and Autopilot—owns. 
 Copilot Chat 
 Work with you
 Interactive reasoning
 Work alongside you in the flow of everyday work
 Cowork 
 Work for you
 Execute delegated tasks
 Take on scoped, multistep work you delegate
 Autopilot 
 Work as a teammate
 Own ongoing work
 Work with its own identity and lifecycle, sponsored by you
 Copilot Chat assists in the flow of everyday work. Cowork can carry a complex assignment across multiple steps and applications. Autopilot adds a new layer—it can handle ongoing work that unfolds across days and weeks: monitoring priorities, coordinating schedules, tracking commitments, preparing recurring updates, and moving stalled tasks forward.
 “You talk to your Autopilot in Teams or Outlook, and you delegate work to it exactly as you would a human. You don’t have to use or learn a new interaction paradigm.”
 Alex Weingart, principal product manager, Microsoft Teams 
 Like a colleague working closely with you on an important project, Autopilot is personal, proactive, and always on.
 This familiar interaction model matters because employees don’t have to learn a separate way to collaborate and delegate. They can message or mention Autopilot just like they would ping a colleague.
 “You talk to your Autopilot in Teams or Outlook, and you delegate work to it exactly as you would a human,” says Alex Weingart, a principal product manager for Microsoft Teams. “You don’t have to use or learn a new interaction paradigm.”
 When delegating is as easy as sending a message, employees start handing off more—especially the repetitive coordination that fills so much of an information worker’s day. Over time, Autopilot stops feeling like something employees use and starts feeling like someone they work with.
 “This is the start of a new relationship between human employees and their agents. With Autopilot, it’s really about taking the manual labor out of information work.”
 Adam Sheppard, principal product manager, Autopilot 
 That shift is exactly what the Autopilot product team targeted and designed for. Instead of waiting for a prompt, Autopilot keeps tabs on commitments, nudges stalled tasks, and gets recurring updates ready on its own schedule—work that used to depend on someone remembering to do it. Employees still decide what to delegate and how much latitude to give Autopilot, but they no longer have to carry every loose end themselves.
 “This is the start of a new relationship between human employees and their agents,” says Adam Sheppard, principal product manager for Autopilot. “With Autopilot, it’s really about taking the manual labor out of information work.”
 But the same qualities that make personal agents like Autopilot useful also create a new administrative requirement. Organizations can’t govern an always-on agent with a mailbox, storage, memory, and access to work resources the same way they would an application.
 To support and secure their work, the organization needs to apply identity, security, compliance, and lifecycle controls behind the experience. That’s why each Autopilot gets a user-like identity, a clearly accountable human sponsor, and a defined business purpose.
 Behind that familiar experience is a deliberately different identity model. In a one-to-one interaction, Autopilot can use the sponsor’s context. In a group setting, it operates under its own identity and remains limited to the context and tools available in that shared space.
 This separation helps prevent private information from crossing into a multiplayer conversation, while retaining the convenience people expect in a personal exchange.
 Building accountability into identity
 For our identity team, an agent user creates a control point for answering basic enterprise questions: What is this agent? Who’s accountable for it? What can it access? What does it do? When should it stop operating?
 Every one of those answers traces back to a named human sponsor.
 “We don’t want autonomy to remove responsibility. Every agent user needs to be accountable to a human.”
 Ramanan Hariharan, principal engineering manager, Agentic Identity and Access Management 
 A separate identity also makes it possible to distinguish an employee’s actions from the agent’s actions, preserve audit records, block the agent without blocking the employee, and connect retirement to changes in the sponsor’s role or employment status. We’re also developing monitoring and enforcement around inactivity, ownership, provisioning, and deprovisioning as the pilot expands.
 “We don’t want autonomy to remove responsibility,” says Ramanan Hariharan, a principal engineering manager of Agentic Identity and Access Management at Microsoft. “Every agent user needs to be accountable to a human.”
 Managing the template and every agent user it creates
 As we have experimented with Autopilot, we have also needed to calibrate two levels of administration. The product or agent template is one governance object. Each employee’s Autopilot is a separate operational instance with its own identity and lifecycle.
 At enterprise scale, administrators need visibility at both levels: which templates we’ve approved, how many instances exist, active or inactive status, who sponsors them, what access they have, and whether we should pause, restore, or remove them.
 This is where Microsoft Agent 365 and the broader Microsoft 365 control environment come together:
 AI administrators have a unified inventory and the ability to take immediate action.
 Identity administrators manage provisioning and lifecycle controls in Microsoft Entra.
 Microsoft Purview supports audit and data protection.
 Microsoft Defender contributes security monitoring.
 The operating model is collaborative by design because no single administrative discipline owns the entire agent user lifecycle.
 Starting with least privilege and earning autonomy
 During our pilot, we’ve treated access as a decision rather than an inheritance.
 Because Autopilot has its own identity, it starts with access to nothing. It isn’t automatically added to the same groups or given the same permissions its sponsor has. That’s a safety advantage, but it also means someone has to grant access to each resource it needs, just as they would for a new team member.
 The sponsor or administrator grants the access Autopilot needs for its work, and the organization can apply higher-priority tenant policies. In shared conversations, Autopilot is limited to the context of the meeting, channel, or group chat and to a narrower set of tools.
 “The human is still in control. The assistant is helping the employee be successful.”
 David Johnson, governance and architecture lead, Microsoft Digital 
 This approach supports a graduated model of autonomy. An employee can begin with review checkpoints and narrow permissions, then expand the boundaries as the agent demonstrates reliable behavior. Meanwhile, administrators retain the ability to observe activity and pause or remove an instance when necessary.
 “The human is still in control,” says David Johnson, who leads governance and architecture work for personal agents in Microsoft Digital. “The assistant is helping the employee be successful.”
 The practical goal isn’t autonomy for its own sake. It’s dependable help within understandable boundaries. Those boundaries have to work for the employee directing Autopilot and for the teams responsible for identity, data, security, cost, and service health.
 Building controls into the product
 Many of these boundaries depend on controls that are still taking shape. During the pilot, we’ve filled some gaps with temporary, internal solutions. That’s been enough to keep the pilot running safely, but it isn’t something we’d want to carry to every employee or ask customers to rebuild for themselves.
 “We don’t want customers to have to create IT glue. Our experience is helping us develop what we embed in the product and where customers need flexibility.”
 Eileen Zhou, principal product manager, Microsoft Digital 
 Getting this right for every employee is where our focus is now: governing Autopilots across their full lifecycle at scale, from provisioning, sponsorship, and access to compliance and offboarding. That’s where being Customer Zero pays off. When we find a gap in our own environment, the question isn’t only how to close it. It’s whether the fix belongs in the product, where every customer gets it, or in policy that each organization sets for itself.
 “We don’t want customers to have to create IT glue,” says Eileen Zhou, principal product manager in Microsoft Digital. “Our experience is helping us develop what we embed in the product and where customers need flexibility.”
 How employees are using Autopilot
 Adoption during the pilot has been voluntary, and demand has outpaced access. Early users are applying it to scheduling, inbox triage, meeting preparation, status reporting, expense preparation, bug filing, and ongoing monitoring. The common thread: Autopilot is taking on work that repeats, interrupts focus, or needs attention over time.
 The use cases we’re seeing at Microsoft fall into three areas of work:
 1. Daily rhythm: Keeping you on top of your schedule by preparing, prioritizing, and responding as needed.
 Morning briefing: Highlighting the day’s meetings with prep links, overnight emails that need attention, changes to documents, and upcoming deadlines.
 End-of-day wrap: Recapping what you planned to do during your day, calling out what’s still open, and assembling tomorrow’s top three priorities.
 Calendar hygiene: Flagging double-bookings, meetings with no agendas, and back-to-backs with no break, then proposing fixes.
 2. Communications flow: Keeping your inbox and messaging moving without constant manual triage.
 Inbox prioritization on a regular cadence: Surfacing only messages that need your response or decision, grouping the rest by category, and highlighting what’s urgent.
 Replies in your voice: Autopilot drafts messages in your voice for approval and replies as itself (signed as Autopilot) inside a scope you’ve delegated.
 Follow-up tracking: Identifying unanswered threads, missed asks, and outstanding commitments, then nudging owners directly as your Autopilot, so the requests have clear attribution.
 3. Getting work done: Driving work through to completion across meetings, messages, and tasks.
 Document preparation: Proactively preparing recurring documents, like pre-reads or stats reports on a trigger or schedule.
 Multistep workflows: Managing repeatable processes, like triaging escalations and coordinating reviews end to end.
 Cross-team coordination: Pulling in the right people, sharing context, and keeping work moving without manual orchestration.
 Because each Autopilot has its own identity, it can also do things a typical tool can’t. Here are three examples:
 Autopilot’s own Outlook mailbox and Teams presence: Other employees can email, @-mention, or chat with Autopilot directly. For example, a colleague could message “Ask Eileen’s Autopilot for the latest status,” and Autopilot answers without routing through its sponsor.
 Covering for employees while they’re out of the office: Autopilot stays in threads and answers routine asks within its delegated scope.
 Joining meetings as a participant: Autopilot attends, takes notes, or represents its sponsor’s status in a standup as itself.
 Preparing for the personal agent era
 Deploying Autopilot to more employees across Microsoft marks the point where personal agents become part of how our whole company works. It’s also a preview of what’s ahead for every enterprise.
 As personal agents become regular participants in enterprise systems, organizations will need to manage not only what they can do, but also who sponsors them, how they put boundaries around their access, how they audit their work, and how they leave the environment when their purpose ends.
 Our Customer Zero experience can give you an early look at the decisions that come with expanding access. Think of this as the first pages of our Autopilot playbook. We’ll keep sharing it as we write it, including a deployment guide in early 2027.
 Key takeaways
 As you prepare for always-on personal agents in your own environments, keep these actions in mind:
 Assign a human sponsor and a clear business purpose to every personal agent.
 Separate template governance from the lifecycle of each operational agent instance.
 Start with least privilege access and only expand when a scenario requires it.
 Coordinate AI, identity, data, security, service, and finance administrators before scaling.
 Model identity volume before you scale. Plan for what one agent identity per employee means for your directory, mailboxes, storage, and collaboration services.
 Plan for provisioning, inactivity reviews, sponsor changes, blocking, restoration, and retirement.
 Use pilots to determine which controls belong in the product and which require organization-specific policy.
